title: Java Slide 6
description: Practice test covering Java static methods, method-call stacks, argument promotion, SecureRandom, enum types, scope, and method overloading.

questions.prompt: Review the following Java code. What is the exact result when this program is executed?
questions.explanation: Math.abs(-5.5) evaluates to 5.5. Math.floor(5.9) evaluates to the largest integer not greater than 5.9, which is 5.0. Math.max(5.5, 5.0) returns the larger value, resulting in 5.5.

questions.prompt: Analyze the following snippet that uses an enum type to track game status. What is the exact output?
questions.explanation: Java does not allow an int literal or variable to be directly compared to an enum constant. Attempting to use the '==' operator between an int and an enum type causes a compilation error.

questions.prompt: Look at the method overloading example below. What exact string will be printed to the console?
questions.explanation: The literal 7 is treated as an int. The compiler successfully matches this exactly to the method signature requiring an int, so it invokes the printVal(int x) method.

questions.prompt: Evaluate the scope of the variables in the following code block. What is the exact result?
questions.explanation: The local variable x is declared inside the block of the for loop. Its scope ends exactly at the closing brace of that block, making it inaccessible to the print statement outside, causing a compilation error.

questions.prompt: Review the usage of SecureRandom below. What is the exact output of this program?
questions.explanation: The nextInt(int x) method returns a random integer from 0 up to, but excluding, the value of x. Therefore, nextInt(1) will exclusively return 0. Adding 5 results deterministically in 5.

questions.prompt: Determine the exact printed output based on Java's string concatenation rules.
questions.explanation: Java evaluates the '+' operator left-to-right. First, 3 + 4 evaluates to 7. Then, 7 is concatenated with " and " yielding "7 and ". Next, "7 and " + 3 yields "7 and 3", and finally adding 4 yields "7 and 34".

questions.prompt: Consider how Java handles argument promotion and casting in the following code. What is the exact output?
questions.explanation: The integer a is cast to a float (5.0f). However, the literal 0.5 is a double by default. During addition, the float is promoted to the higher type (double). The result is a double, which safely calls the print(double x) method.

questions.prompt: Observe the interaction between the class field and the local variable. What is the exact output of this program?
questions.explanation: The modify method declares a local variable x, which temporarily shadows the class field x. The multiplication modifies only the local variable. The class field x is unaffected and remains 10 when printed in main.

questions.prompt: Examine the overloaded method declarations below. What is the exact outcome when attempting to run this class?
questions.explanation: The compiler distinguishes overloaded methods strictly by their signature (name and parameters). Return types are not considered part of the signature. Declaring two methods with identical parameter lists causes a compilation error.

questions.prompt: Carefully trace the recursive execution of the factorial method. What is the exact result?
questions.explanation: The recursive method call passes n instead of n - 1. Because the parameter never decreases, it will never reach the base case of n == 0. This results in infinite method calls, eventually exhausting the method-call stack.
